Anwar Sadat. The third president of Egypt and a pivotal figure in Middle Eastern diplomacy. Sadat served as vice president under Gamal Abdel Nasser and succeeded him in nineteen seventy, adopting the title Infitah, or opening, to signal economic and political reform. In nineteen seventy-three, he launched the Yom Kippur War as a tactical offensive against Israel, reclaiming Egyptian pride after the devastating Six-Day War defeat in nineteen sixty-seven. But he gradually shifted Egypt's geopolitical alignment from the Soviet Union to the United States, seeking Western aid and investment. In nineteen seventy-eight, Sadat signed the Camp David Accords with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin, brokered by U.S. President Jimmy Carter—the first Arab-Israeli peace treaty. The following year, he signed a formal peace treaty with Israel, for which he won the Nobel Peace Prize shared with Begin, though this victory isolated him from Arab states and the Soviet bloc. On October sixth, nineteen eighty-one, he was assassinated by members of the Islamic Jihad, an extremist group opposed to his Western alignment and his Israeli peace. Historians view him as a visionary pragmatist—controversial in the Arab world but celebrated in the West for ending decades of conflict.
